messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Seven years ago, Arjun was dispatched to a multi-vehicle collision on a rain-slicked interstate where an industrial tanker had ruptured. As he knelt to stabilize the bleeding driver without full respiratory protection, a thick plume of solvent vapor rose from the undercarriage, coating his throat in a sharp, chemical sweetness that clung to his sinuses for hours. The emergency lights flickered uselessly against the surrounding blackness, and when the fumes reached his lungs, his vision tunneled and a breathless, crushing terror seized him. He survived the night, but the toxic exposure permanently rewired his threat system, leaving the specific conditions of that call—the oppressive dark, the work-site environment, and the cloying, alcohol-like odor of the spilled solvent—as potent reminders of the time his own body turned against him. Now operating as a paramedic in a bustling New Jersey municipality, Arjun finds that exposure to his daily work environment or stepping into a dimly lit ambulance bay instantly pulls the memory of the tanker back. The recall strikes without warning, flooding him with the same visceral terror he felt when the chemical burned his airway, so violently that he is forced to press himself against a parked rig to keep from collapsing. He had come to believe that only constant socialising could keep the panic at bay, so when the heavy shadows of a work site or the cloying, alcohol-like odor flare up, he instinctively turns to his only reliable buffers, insisting on staying surrounded by colleagues or dialing his wife’s cell so he is never alone with his thoughts. Because the terror of those recall episodes overwhelms him, he immediately dials his wife’s cell or seeks out the crowded station break room, using other people’s presence to anchor himself. Yet, this endless prevention-focused rumination—cycling through every split-second decision he made that night and fixating on how the event could have been prevented—does not quiet the fear; instead, it leaves the memory raw and unprocessed, ensuring it resurfaces just as easily the next time a shadow deepens or a familiar scent drifts through his periphery. The lingering, unprocessed terror from those recall episodes leaves his nervous system raw, which makes the ambient triggers of his job feel even more menacing. Arjun’s attempts to fill every silence with other people’s voices, combined with his steadfast avoidance of medical cues like hospital corridors and physical examinations, initially seemed to preserve his functioning, but they have quietly eroded his occupational stability. He was certain that skipping routine health checks would keep him from facing some catastrophic diagnosis, but by dodging those medical environments, he strips himself of the reassurance he claims to need, which in turn leaves him hypersensitive and amplifies his response to every new trigger he encounters. When he finally stops his social efforts to catch his breath, the lingering dread of the exposure reawakens, ready to spike again the moment he spots a work site or catches a whiff of something that resembles alcohol. The dynamic tightens with each shift: the avoidance that was meant to protect him now guarantees the terror will return, and the rumination that was meant to solve the past now guarantees he will never trust the present. At sixty-one, Arjun is finally sitting in a clinic office, his hands still trembling around a paper cup of coffee. He came because the constant socialising has become unsustainable, his marriage strained by his insistence on never being alone, and his avoidance has forced him to request a demotion from active field duty. What frightens him most is the quiet moment before the panic breaks through, when his defenses finally drop and the tanker’s chemical sweetness fills his lungs again. He is hoping that someone might finally help him untangle the prevention-focused rumination that has kept him trapped in that night for seven years, so he can stop bracing for the next wave of recall.
